::: callout-note
## tl;dr

A simple, interpretable model fit to features representing football concepts predicted as well as a neural network fit to player tracking data.
:::

## The inspo

I came across a [sports analytics project shared online in 2025](https://medium.com/@lou.j.dimuro/predicting-nfl-short-pass-success-with-a-cnn-2f279c985769) by [Lou DiMuro](https://www.linkedin.com/in/lou-dimuro/) that I really liked. It uses NFL player tracking data from the start of the 2021 and 2022 seasons to estimate, for plays where the QB throws a completed short pass, the probability the play will be successful. A short pass here is one where the receiver is at most 2 yards past the line of scrimmage when the ball is released. It has an awesome GIF showing the players' movement as a play progresses with a live updating estimate (obviously inspired my video above). Very cool.

What counts as a 'successful' play in their analysis depends on the down:

- On **1st down**, the play needs to **gain ≥ 40%** of the yards needed for a new set of downs
- On **2nd down**, it needs to **gain ≥ 60%**
- On **3rd or 4th down**, it needs to **gain 100%**

What's interesting is that the model needs to account for the yards a receiver might gain after the catch, which aren't known at the time of the pass. It's judged on the outcome of the entire play (not just the pass). Only completed passes are included (no incompletions or interceptions), so it's essentially asking "will the play gain enough yards assuming it's caught?"

It uses a [convolutional](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KuXjwB4LzSA&t=87s) [neural network](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rEDzUT3ymw4) (CNN) to estimate the probability of a successful play at the moment the ball is released. A strength of CNNs is that they can learn patterns from complex, high-dimensional inputs (e.g., position and velocity of all 22 players on the field). This comes at the cost of some interpretability. They can be very good at recognising situations that make a pass more or less likely to succeed, but understanding why the likelihood changes or how much different aspects of the play contribute to it is hard.

Whether interpretability like this matters depends on what we want from the model. If the main goal is pure prediction, giving a flexible model access to the full tracking data makes sense. But in applied sport environments, analysts also need to explain and discuss predictions with coaches or players who need to make decisions and actually do things in the game. Those conversations often turn to what might have happened if someone did something differently.

A coach wants to know: 

> If I ask a player to instead do it *this* way, what can I expect to change?

An athlete watching film might think: 

> If I do *this*, how might the defenders respond and how would that impact the play?

These are causal questions that can't be answered from observational play data alone. What can be done though, is to represent the plays in football terms and examine how those representations relate to success. For example:

> How does the space around a receiver at the time of the pass relate to the probability of a successful play?
>
> How does the nearest defender's closing speed relate to the chance of success?

Putting the questions in football terms like this gives coaches and players something concrete to challenge. They might disagree with how I've represented space or closing speed conceptually, or whether the relationships found make sense to them based on their domain knowledge. That discussion might uncover something worth testing with a research design that can estimate a causal effect.

My aim here is to turn the data used to train the CNN into a small set of domain-informed "football features" (e.g., space around a receiver, blocker positioning, etc) and use Bayesian [logistic regression](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yIYKR4sgzI8&t=343s) to model the probability of success. The features make my choices about how to represent the play explicit, the regression model makes the relationships easier to inspect, and the Bayesian approach lets me quantify and carry the uncertainty in those relationships through to the predicted probability of success. 

The question is whether the transparency gained by making those football concepts explicit costs much in predictive performance.

## Python code outputs will differ from rendered results

The charts and tables on this page are made by the R code. The Python code runs the same analysis, but its charts are much simpler (no annotations or custom styling) and its tables use great_tables' defaults. R and Python also use different random number generators and samplers (Stan through CmdStanR in R, PyMC in Python), so the exact numbers won't match. The statistical results (the model's estimates, the cross-validated scores and the probabilities) should be the same within the noise of random sampling.
:::

The raw tracking data comes from the [NFL's Next Gen Stats Big Data Bowl](https://operations.nfl.com/programs-initiatives/innovation/big-data-bowl). The data is available on [Kaggle](https://www.kaggle.com), split across two competitions. [Big Data Bowl 2023](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/nfl-big-data-bowl-2023) contains data from weeks 1–8 of the 2021 season and [Big Data Bowl 2025](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/nfl-big-data-bowl-2025) has weeks 1–9 of the 2022 season.

With ~50 frames per play and the position of every player and ball recorded at each frame, the full tracking dataset is ~3.7M rows. You can download it with a free Kaggle account after joining each competition and accepting the rules.

I didn't work directly from the raw Kaggle data. I used the preprocessed data from [Lou's project GitHub repo](https://github.com/ldimuro/NFL-Short-Pass-Success-Probability), which captures only the completed short pass plays and transforms the data into tensors suitable for modelling with a neural network. It includes 3,228 plays, and 59% of them were successful. Instead of re-publishing the full 100+ MB dataset, I've included one play in the reference repo's format as an example to demonstrate how I transformed it.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## ![R](/img/Rlogo.svg){height="25"}

```{r}
#| label: reshape
#| code-summary: "R code · turning the reference format into tables"
example_play <- read_rds(file.path(data_url, "example_play_tensor.rds"))

flatten_play_data <- function(tensors) {
  defender_rows <- expand_grid(
    play_row = seq_len(dim(tensors)[1]),
    defender_slot = seq_len(dim(tensors)[3])
  ) |>
    mutate(
      # The reference format stores each velocity as (y, x), not (x, y)
      defender_velocity_x = tensors[
        cbind(play_row, 2L, defender_slot, 1L)
      ],
      defender_velocity_y = tensors[
        cbind(play_row, 1L, defender_slot, 1L)
      ],
      defender_offset_downfield = tensors[cbind(
        play_row,
        3L,
        defender_slot,
        1L
      )],
      defender_offset_lateral = tensors[
        cbind(play_row, 4L, defender_slot, 1L)
      ],
      defender_velocity_relative_x = tensors[cbind(
        play_row,
        6L,
        defender_slot,
        1L
      )],
      defender_velocity_relative_y = tensors[cbind(
        play_row,
        5L,
        defender_slot,
        1L
      )]
    ) |>
    filter_out(defender_offset_downfield == 0, defender_offset_lateral == 0)

  blocker_rows <- expand_grid(
    play_row = seq_len(dim(tensors)[1]),
    defender_slot = seq_len(dim(tensors)[3]),
    offender_slot = seq_len(dim(tensors)[4])
  ) |>
    semi_join(defender_rows, by = join_by(play_row, defender_slot)) |>
    mutate(
      offender_offset_downfield = tensors[cbind(
        play_row,
        7L,
        defender_slot,
        offender_slot
      )],
      offender_offset_lateral = tensors[cbind(
        play_row,
        8L,
        defender_slot,
        offender_slot
      )],
      offender_velocity_relative_downfield = tensors[cbind(
        play_row,
        10L,
        defender_slot,
        offender_slot
      )],
      offender_velocity_relative_lateral = tensors[cbind(
        play_row,
        9L,
        defender_slot,
        offender_slot
      )]
    ) |>
    filter_out(offender_offset_downfield == 0, offender_offset_lateral == 0)

  play_context <- tibble(
    play_row = seq_len(dim(tensors)[1]),
    down = tensors[, 11L, 1L, 1L] * 3,
    yards_to_go = tensors[, 12L, 1L, 1L] * 29.5 + 0.5
  ) |>
    mutate(
      down = pmin(4L, pmax(1L, round(down))),
      # The yardage the play actually has to gain, given the down.
      yards_needed = recode_values(down, 1 ~ 0.4, 2 ~ 0.6, default = 1) *
        yards_to_go
    )

  list(
    defenders = defender_rows,
    blockers = blocker_rows,
    context = play_context
  )
}

tabular_play <- flatten_play_data(example_play)
```

## ![Python](/img/python-logo-only.svg){height="30"}

```{python}
#| eval: false
#| code-summary: "Python code · turning the reference format into tables"


def read_rds(url):
    """An array saved from R as .rds, and its attributes."""
    with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(suffix=".rds") as file:
        urllib.request.urlretrieve(url, file.name)
        parsed = rdata.parser.parse_file(file.name)
    converter = rdata.conversion.SimpleConverter()
    return converter.convert(parsed.object), converter.convert(parsed.object.attributes)


example_play, example_attributes = read_rds(f"{DATA_URL}/example_play_tensor.rds")


def flatten_play_data(tensors):
    n_plays, _, n_defenders, n_offence = tensors.shape

    def both_zero(prefix):
        return (pl.col(f"{prefix}_offset_downfield") == 0) & (
            pl.col(f"{prefix}_offset_lateral") == 0
        )

    play_row, defender_slot = np.meshgrid(
        np.arange(n_plays), np.arange(n_defenders), indexing="ij"
    )

    def defender(channel):
        return tensors[:, channel, :, 0].ravel()

    defender_rows = pl.DataFrame(
        {
            "play_row": play_row.ravel(),
            "defender_slot": defender_slot.ravel(),
            # The reference format stores each velocity as (y, x), not (x, y)
            "defender_velocity_x": defender(1),
            "defender_velocity_y": defender(0),
            "defender_offset_downfield": defender(2),
            "defender_offset_lateral": defender(3),
            "defender_velocity_relative_x": defender(5),
            "defender_velocity_relative_y": defender(4),
        }
    ).filter(~both_zero("defender"))

    play_row, defender_slot, offender_slot = np.meshgrid(
        np.arange(n_plays), np.arange(n_defenders), np.arange(n_offence), indexing="ij"
    )

    def offender(channel):
        return tensors[:, channel, :, :].ravel()

    blocker_rows = (
        pl.DataFrame(
            {
                "play_row": play_row.ravel(),
                "defender_slot": defender_slot.ravel(),
                "offender_slot": offender_slot.ravel(),
                "offender_offset_downfield": offender(6),
                "offender_offset_lateral": offender(7),
                "offender_velocity_relative_downfield": offender(9),
                "offender_velocity_relative_lateral": offender(8),
            }
        )
        .join(
            defender_rows.select("play_row", "defender_slot"),
            on=["play_row", "defender_slot"],
            how="semi",
        )
        .filter(~both_zero("offender"))
    )

    play_context = (
        pl.DataFrame(
            {
                "play_row": np.arange(n_plays),
                "down": tensors[:, 10, 0, 0] * 3,
                "yards_to_go": tensors[:, 11, 0, 0] * 29.5 + 0.5,
            }
        )
        .with_columns(down=pl.col("down").round().clip(1, 4).cast(pl.Int64))
        .with_columns(
            # The yardage the play actually has to gain, given the down
            yards_needed=pl.col("down").replace_strict({1: 0.4, 2: 0.6}, default=1.0)
            * pl.col("yards_to_go")
        )
    )

    return {
        "defenders": defender_rows,
        "blockers": blocker_rows,
        "context": play_context,
    }


tabular_play = flatten_play_data(example_play)
```
:::

Here's that play at the moment of release. Jacksonville Jaguars' Trevor Lawrence passes to Jamal Agnew, who is 6.5 yards behind the line of scrimmage on 1st & 10 and gains 5. The reference format stores every player relative to the receiver, so Agnew is the fixed point everything is measured from.

#| output: false
#| fig-width: 8

dictionary <- read_csv(
  file.path(data_url, "feature_dictionary.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

final_features <- dictionary |> pull(feature)

plays <- read_csv(
  file.path(data_url, "short_pass_features.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

example_published <- plays |>
  filter(
    game_id == attr(example_play, "game_id"),
    play_id == attr(example_play, "play_id")
  )

plotted_defenders <- tabular_play |>
  pluck("defenders") |>
  mutate(
    distance = sqrt(defender_offset_downfield^2 + defender_offset_lateral^2),
    nearest = distance == min(distance)
  )

# Offensive players are stored relative to each defender, so one defender's
# copy is enough to place them
offence <- tabular_play$blockers |>
  slice_min(defender_slot, by = offender_slot) |>
  left_join(
    plotted_defenders |>
      select(defender_slot, defender_offset_downfield, defender_offset_lateral),
    by = join_by(defender_slot)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    lateral = defender_offset_lateral + offender_offset_lateral,
    downfield = defender_offset_downfield + offender_offset_downfield
  )

nearest_defender <- plotted_defenders |> filter(nearest)
line_of_scrimmage <- -example_published$receiver_depth
success_line <- line_of_scrimmage + example_published$yards_needed
field_edge <- min(plotted_defenders$defender_offset_lateral, offence$lateral) -
  1

# The brackets sit in a column to the right of the field
margin_x <- max(plotted_defenders$defender_offset_lateral, offence$lateral) +
  2.5

quarterback <- offence |> slice_min(downfield)

ordinal <- c("1st", "2nd", "3rd", "4th")

yards <- \(x) {
  x |>
    abs() |>
    scales::number(accuracy = 0.1, trim = TRUE) |>
    str_remove("\\.0$")
}

share_needed <- recode_values(
  example_published$down,
  1 ~ "40% of",
  2 ~ "60% of",
  c(3, 4) ~ "all of",
  unmatched = "error"
)

brackets <- tibble(
  bottom = c(0, line_of_scrimmage),
  top = c(line_of_scrimmage, success_line),
  label = c(
    str_glue(
      "Receiver {yards(line_of_scrimmage)} yards\nbehind the line"
    ),
    str_glue(
      "{yards(example_published$yards_needed)} yards needed\n({share_needed} the",
      " {example_published$yards_to_go} to\ngo on {ordinal[example_published$down]} down)"
    )
  )
)

field_green <- "#D7E8DC"
dark_green <- "#166534"

field <- tibble(
  xmin = field_edge - 0.5,

)

yard_lines <- tibble(

) |>

```{python}
#| eval: false

dictionary = pl.read_csv(f"{DATA_URL}/feature_dictionary.csv")

final_features = dictionary["feature"].to_list()

plays = pl.read_csv(f"{DATA_URL}/short_pass_features.csv")

example_published = plays.filter(
    pl.col("game_id") == int(example_attributes["game_id"][0]),
    pl.col("play_id") == int(example_attributes["play_id"][0]),
)

plotted_defenders = (
    tabular_play["defenders"]
    .with_columns(
        distance=(
            pl.col("defender_offset_downfield") ** 2
            + pl.col("defender_offset_lateral") ** 2
        ).sqrt()
    )
    .with_columns(nearest=pl.col("distance") == pl.col("distance").min())
)

# Offensive players are stored relative to each defender, so one defender's
# copy is enough to place them
offence = (
    tabular_play["blockers"]
    .filter(
        pl.col("defender_slot") == pl.col("defender_slot").min().over("offender_slot")
    )
    .join(
        plotted_defenders.select(
            "defender_slot", "defender_offset_downfield", "defender_offset_lateral"
        ),
        on="defender_slot",
    )
    .with_columns(
        lateral=pl.col("defender_offset_lateral") + pl.col("offender_offset_lateral"),
        downfield=pl.col("defender_offset_downfield")
        + pl.col("offender_offset_downfield"),
    )
)

line_of_scrimmage = -example_published["receiver_depth"].item()
success_line = line_of_scrimmage + example_published["yards_needed"].item()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 6))
ax.axhline(line_of_scrimmage, color="grey", label="Line of scrimmage")
ax.axhline(
    success_line, color="green", linestyle="--", label="A successful play gets here"
)
# Where each defender will be in half a second at their current rate
ax.quiver(
    plotted_defenders["defender_offset_lateral"],
    plotted_defenders["defender_offset_downfield"],
    plotted_defenders["defender_velocity_y"] / 2,
    plotted_defenders["defender_velocity_x"] / 2,
    angles="xy",
    scale_units="xy",
    scale=1,
    width=0.004,
    color="grey",
)
ax.scatter(
    offence["lateral"], offence["downfield"], s=80, facecolor="white", edgecolor=NAVY
)
ax.scatter(
    plotted_defenders["defender_offset_lateral"],
    plotted_defenders["defender_offset_downfield"],
    s=80,

ax.scatter(0, 0, s=100, color=NAVY, label="Receiver")

## The football features

With the tracking data in a simple tabular format, I can start creating features that describe the play in football terms. Instead of feeding the model every player's position and velocity directly, I define things that I think might matter (e.g., how far the nearest defender is from the receiver and how quickly they're closing that space).

The data says where the receiver and defenders are, but I'm deciding which football concepts within those measurements might inform the outcome. Someone with a different view of the game might choose differently. That's a limitation, but it also puts the assumptions out in the open.

The simplest example is yards needed. The CNN was given the down and distance and had to learn the success rule from the data. I already know the rule, so I just calculated the yards each play needs and gave the model that instead.

The model I built uses nine features covering six concepts:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## ![R](/img/Rlogo.svg){height="25"}

```{r}
#| output: false
#| code-summary: "R code · calculate and show the features"

# The features for every play in a set of tables from flatten_play_data(),
# one row per play
# receiver_depth comes separately from the season play data, not the tensors.
# The line of scrimmage is at x = 60 after preprocessing, so receiver_depth
# is the receiver's x position at release minus 60 (positive beyond the line).
calculate_features <- function(tables) {
  defenders <- tables$defenders |>
    mutate(
      distance = sqrt(defender_offset_downfield^2 + defender_offset_lateral^2),
      # How fast the gap to the receiver is shrinking (positive is closing):
      # the relative velocity along the line between them
      closing_speed = -(defender_offset_downfield *
        defender_velocity_relative_x +
        defender_offset_lateral * defender_velocity_relative_y) /
        (distance + 1e-6)
    )

  around_the_receiver <- defenders |>
    summarise(
      # The nearest defender in front of the receiver, or the farthest
      # defender if nobody is in front
      space_ahead = if (any(defender_offset_downfield > 0)) {
        min(distance[defender_offset_downfield > 0])
      } else {
        max(distance)
      },
      room_beyond_nearest = space_ahead - min(distance),
      min_def_y_distance_to_rec = min(abs(defender_offset_lateral)),
      nearest_def_cushion = defender_offset_downfield[which.min(distance)],
      def_y_spread = sd(defender_offset_lateral),
      mean_top3_closing_speed = mean(head(closing_speed[order(distance)], 3)),
      nearest_defender = defender_slot[which.min(distance)],
      .by = play_row
    )

  # The nearest defender's closest offensive player, and their relative speed
  blockers <- tables$blockers |>
    inner_join(
      around_the_receiver |> select(play_row, defender_slot = nearest_defender),
      by = join_by(play_row, defender_slot)
    ) |>
    mutate(
      distance = sqrt(offender_offset_downfield^2 + offender_offset_lateral^2),
      relative_speed = sqrt(
        offender_velocity_relative_downfield^2 +
          offender_velocity_relative_lateral^2
      )
    ) |>
    summarise(
      nearest_blocker_advantage = min(distance),
      nearest_blocker_relative_speed = relative_speed[which.min(distance)],
      .by = play_row
    )

  tables$context |>
    select(play_row, yards_needed) |>
    left_join(
      around_the_receiver |> select(-space_ahead, -nearest_defender),
      by = join_by(play_row)
    ) |>
    left_join(blockers, by = join_by(play_row))
}

example_features <- calculate_features(tabular_play) |>
  pivot_longer(-play_row, names_to = "feature", values_to = "calculated") |>
  left_join(
    example_published |>
      select(all_of(setdiff(final_features, "receiver_depth"))) |>
      pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "feature", values_to = "published"),
    by = join_by(feature)
  )

if (
  !isTRUE(all.equal(example_features$calculated, example_features$published))
) {
  cli::cli_abort("The features calculated here don't match the published ones.")
}

features_table <- dictionary |>

  cols_label(label = "Feature", description = "What it measures") |>
  cols_width(group ~ pct(19), label ~ pct(29)) |>
  tab_style(

    locations = cells_body(columns = label)
  ) |>

  )

```

## ![Python](/img/python-logo-only.svg){height="30"}

```{python}
#| eval: false
#| code-summary: "Python code · calculate and show the features"

# The features for every play in a set of tables from flatten_play_data(),
# one row per play
# receiver_depth comes separately from the season play data, not the tensors.
# The line of scrimmage is at x = 60 after preprocessing, so receiver_depth
# is the receiver's x position at release minus 60 (positive beyond the line).
def calculate_features(tables):
    distance = (
        pl.col("defender_offset_downfield") ** 2
        + pl.col("defender_offset_lateral") ** 2
    ).sqrt()
    defenders = (
        tables["defenders"]
        .with_columns(distance=distance)
        .with_columns(
            # How fast the gap to the receiver is shrinking (positive is closing):
            # the relative velocity along the line between them
            closing_speed=-(
                pl.col("defender_offset_downfield")
                * pl.col("defender_velocity_relative_x")
                + pl.col("defender_offset_lateral")
                * pl.col("defender_velocity_relative_y")
            )
            / (pl.col("distance") + 1e-6)
        )
    )

    nearest = pl.col("distance").arg_min()
    in_front = pl.col("defender_offset_downfield") > 0
    around_the_receiver = (
        defenders.group_by("play_row")
        .agg(
            # The nearest defender in front of the receiver, or the farthest
            # defender if nobody is in front
            space_ahead=pl.when(in_front.any())
            .then(pl.col("distance").filter(in_front).min())
            .otherwise(pl.col("distance").max()),
            closest=pl.col("distance").min(),
            min_def_y_distance_to_rec=pl.col("defender_offset_lateral").abs().min(),
            nearest_def_cushion=pl.col("defender_offset_downfield").get(nearest),
            def_y_spread=pl.col("defender_offset_lateral").std(),
            mean_top3_closing_speed=pl.col("closing_speed")
            .sort_by("distance", maintain_order=True)
            .head(3)
            .mean(),
            nearest_defender=pl.col("defender_slot").get(nearest),
        )
        .with_columns(room_beyond_nearest=pl.col("space_ahead") - pl.col("closest"))
    )

    # The nearest defender's closest offensive player, and their relative speed
    blocker_distance = (
        pl.col("offender_offset_downfield") ** 2
        + pl.col("offender_offset_lateral") ** 2
    ).sqrt()
    blockers = (
        tables["blockers"]
        .join(
            around_the_receiver.select(
                "play_row", defender_slot=pl.col("nearest_defender")
            ),
            on=["play_row", "defender_slot"],
        )
        .with_columns(
            distance=blocker_distance,
            relative_speed=(
                pl.col("offender_velocity_relative_downfield") ** 2
                + pl.col("offender_velocity_relative_lateral") ** 2
            ).sqrt(),
        )
        .group_by("play_row")
        .agg(
            nearest_blocker_advantage=pl.col("distance").min(),
            nearest_blocker_relative_speed=pl.col("relative_speed").get(nearest),
        )
    )

    return (
        tables["context"]
        .select("play_row", "yards_needed")
        .join(
            around_the_receiver.drop("space_ahead", "closest", "nearest_defender"),
            on="play_row",
            how="left",
        )
        .join(blockers, on="play_row", how="left")
    )


example_features = calculate_features(tabular_play).drop("play_row")

if not np.allclose(
    example_features.to_numpy(),
    example_published.select(example_features.columns).to_numpy(),
):
    raise ValueError("The features calculated here don't match the published ones.")

GT(
    dictionary.select("group", "label", "description"), groupname_col="group"
).cols_label(label="Feature", description="What it measures")
```

## The model

Each play is either successful or it isn't, so I'm modelling the probability of success with logistic regression. The model weights the features, adds their contributions to a baseline, and turns the total into a probability.

The model is written in the probabilistic programming languages [Stan](https://mc-stan.org/) (run from R) and [PyMC](https://www.pymc.io/) (Python).

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## ![R](/img/Rlogo.svg){height="25"}

```{stan}
#| label: stan-model
#| output.var: model
#| cache: true
#| code-summary: "Stan code · the whole model"

// Logistic regression on standardised football features. Two of the
// features (yards needed and the nearest defender's cushion) arrive as natural
// spline columns, built in R, so their effect can bend.

data {
  int<lower=0> N;                    // plays the model learns from
  int<lower=1> K;                    // columns of the design matrix
  matrix[N, K] X;                    // standardised features and spline columns
  array[N] int<lower=0, upper=1> y;  // 1 = successful play

  int<lower=0> N_new;                // plays or frames to score
  matrix[N_new, K] X_new;

  int<lower=0, upper=1> prior_only;  // 1 = ignore the outcomes
}

parameters {
  real alpha;                        // log-odds of success for an average play
  vector[K] beta;                    // change in log-odds per standard deviation
}

model {
  alpha ~ normal(0, 1);
  beta ~ normal(0, 0.35);

  if (!prior_only) {
    y ~ bernoulli_logit_glm(X, alpha, beta);
  }
}

generated quantities {
  // Pointwise log-likelihood, for leave-one-out cross-validation
  vector[N] log_lik;
  // Outcomes the model would expect to see, for predictive checks
  array[N] int y_rep = bernoulli_logit_rng(alpha + X * beta);
  // Probability of success for the plays or frames being scored
  vector[N_new] p_new = inv_logit(alpha + X_new * beta);

  for (n in 1:N) {
    log_lik[n] = bernoulli_logit_lpmf(y[n] | alpha + X[n] * beta);
  }
}
```

## ![Python](/img/python-logo-only.svg){height="30"}

```{python}
#| eval: false
#| code-summary: "Python code · the whole model"

# Logistic regression on standardised football features. Two of the
# features (yards needed and the nearest defender's cushion) arrive as natural
# spline columns (see the next chunk), so their effect can bend.
def build_model(X, y, X_new=None):
    X_new = X.clear() if X_new is None else X_new
    coords = {"column": X.columns, "play": range(X.height), "new": range(X_new.height)}

    with pm.Model(coords=coords) as model:
        # Log-odds of success for an average play
        alpha = pm.Normal("alpha", 0, 1)
        # Change in log-odds per standard deviation
        beta = pm.Normal("beta", 0, 0.35, dims="column")

        pm.Bernoulli(
            "y",
            logit_p=alpha + pm.math.dot(X.to_numpy(), beta),
            observed=y,
            dims="play",
        )
        # Probability of success for the plays or frames being scored
        pm.Deterministic(
            "p_new",
            pm.math.invlogit(alpha + pm.math.dot(X_new.to_numpy(), beta)),
            dims="new",
        )

    return model
```
:::

The model assumes seven of the nine features have a straight-line relationship with the log odds of success. For the other two (yards needed and cushion), I let the model fit a curve (using [splines](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YMl25iCCRew)). This is because going from 1 to 3 yards needed for a successful play is a big deal for a short pass, but 12 to 14 (same +2 yd difference) barely changes the odds (already low). When the nearest defender is close, an extra yard of space can be the difference between a tackle and a catch with room to run. When the defender's already far away or behind the receiver, another yard doesn't change much.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## ![R](/img/Rlogo.svg){height="25"}

```{r}
#| label: design
#| code-summary: "R code · preparing the features for Stan"

# Turn play-level features into the design matrix the Stan model is fitted on.
#
# Everything learned from the training plays (centres, scales and spline knots)
# is kept in a recipe and reused for any other plays or frames, so plays the
# model has not seen never inform their own preprocessing.

SPLINE_TERMS <- c(yards_needed = 4L, nearest_def_cushion = 3L)

design_recipe <- function(train, features, spline_terms = SPLINE_TERMS) {
  linear <- setdiff(features, names(spline_terms))
  bases <- imap(
    spline_terms,
    \(df, feature) splines::ns(train[[feature]], df = df)
  )

  list(
    linear = linear,
    centre = map_dbl(train[linear], mean),
    scale = map_dbl(train[linear], sd),
    bases = bases,
    curve_centre = map(bases, colMeans),
    curve_scale = map(bases, \(basis) map_dbl(as_tibble(basis), sd))
  )
}

design_matrix <- function(plays, recipe) {
  linear <- plays[recipe$linear] |>
    as.matrix() |>
    scale(center = recipe$centre, scale = recipe$scale)

  curves <- imap(recipe$bases, \(basis, feature) {
    curve <- predict(basis, plays[[feature]]) |>
      scale(
        center = recipe$curve_centre[[feature]],
        scale = recipe$curve_scale[[feature]]
      )
    colnames(curve) <- str_c(feature, "_curve", seq_len(ncol(curve)))
    curve
  })

  reduce(curves, cbind, .init = linear)
}

stan_data <- function(train, recipe, new = NULL, prior_only = FALSE) {
  X <- design_matrix(train, recipe)
  X_new <- if (is.null(new)) {
    X[0, , drop = FALSE]
  } else {
    design_matrix(new, recipe)
  }

  list(
    N = nrow(X),
    K = ncol(X),
    X = X,
    y = as.integer(train$success),
    N_new = nrow(X_new),
    X_new = X_new,
    prior_only = as.integer(prior_only)
  )
}

# Centres, scales and curve shapes are learned from the training plays
recipe <- design_recipe(plays, final_features)
```

## ![Python](/img/python-logo-only.svg){height="30"}

```{python}
#| eval: false
#| code-summary: "Python code · preparing the features for the model"

# Turn play-level features into the design matrix the model is fitted on.
#
# Everything learned from the training plays (centres, scales and spline knots)
# is kept in a recipe and reused for any other plays or frames, so plays the
# model has not seen never inform their own preprocessing.

SPLINE_TERMS = {"yards_needed": 4, "nearest_def_cushion": 3}


def natural_spline(x, df):
    """A natural cubic spline for x, Python's usual stand-in for R's
    splines::ns(x, df). Centring the columns leaves the baseline to alpha."""
    spline = f"cr(x, df={df}, constraints='center') - 1"
    return model_matrix(spline, pl.DataFrame({"x": x})).model_spec


def spline_basis(spline, x):
    """The spline's columns at x. Beyond the outer knots the curve carries on
    as a straight line."""
    return np.asarray(spline.get_model_matrix(pl.DataFrame({"x": x})))


def design_recipe(train, features, spline_terms=SPLINE_TERMS):
    linear = [feature for feature in features if feature not in spline_terms]
    splines = {
        feature: natural_spline(train[feature], df)
        for feature, df in spline_terms.items()
    }
    curves = {
        feature: spline_basis(spline, train[feature])
        for feature, spline in splines.items()
    }

    return {
        "linear": linear,
        "centre": {feature: train[feature].mean() for feature in linear},
        "scale": {feature: train[feature].std() for feature in linear},
        "splines": splines,
        "curve_centre": {
            feature: curve.mean(axis=0) for feature, curve in curves.items()
        },
        "curve_scale": {
            feature: curve.std(axis=0, ddof=1) for feature, curve in curves.items()
        },
    }


def design_matrix(plays, recipe):
    linear = plays.select(
        (pl.col(feature) - recipe["centre"][feature]) / recipe["scale"][feature]
        for feature in recipe["linear"]
    )

    curves = []
    for feature, spline in recipe["splines"].items():
        curve = (
            spline_basis(spline, plays[feature]) - recipe["curve_centre"][feature]
        ) / (recipe["curve_scale"][feature])
        names = [f"{feature}_curve{i}" for i in range(1, curve.shape[1] + 1)]
        curves.append(pl.DataFrame(curve, schema=names, orient="row"))

    return pl.concat([linear, *curves], how="horizontal")


# Centres, scales and curve shapes are learned from the training plays
recipe = design_recipe(plays, final_features)

# The training plays as the model sees them
X = design_matrix(plays, recipe)
y = plays["success"].to_numpy()
```
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Prior predictive check and simulation-based calibration (technical details)

**Do the priors make sense?** Bayesian models like this one need priors representing our beliefs about the distribution of plausible parameter values. Because thinking about parameters and understanding their impact on observed outcomes isn't natural to most psychologically well-adjusted humans, it's good practice to simulate outcome data using parameter values drawn from our prior distributions. This way we can see if those choices of priors generate outcome values within the realms of reality. 

In this case, the priors allow a wide range of plausible success rates (about 20–80%) that comfortably includes the observed 59%.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## ![R](/img/Rlogo.svg){height="25"}

```{r}
#| output: false
#| results: hide
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4

prior_fit <- model$sample(
  data = stan_data(plays, recipe, prior_only = TRUE),
  seed = 2534,
  chains = 4,
  parallel_chains = 4,
  iter_warmup = 1000,
  iter_sampling = 1000,
  refresh = 0
)

prior_check <- ppc_stat(
  y = plays$success,
  yrep = prior_fit$draws("y_rep", format = "matrix"),
  stat = "mean",
  binwidth = 0.02
)

# Annotations sit relative to the tallest bar
tallest_bar <- max(layer_data(prior_check, 1)$count)
observed <- mean(plays$success)
simulated_blue <- "#5B80B3"
observed_blue <- "#0D3566"

prior_check_plot <- prior_check +
  annotate(
    "curve",
    x = 0.14,
    xend = 0.27,
    y = 0.82 * tallest_bar,
    yend = 0.6 * tallest_bar,
    curvature = 0.3,
    arrow = arrow(length = unit(2, "mm"), type = "closed"),
    colour = simulated_blue
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = 0.14,
    y = 0.93 * tallest_bar,
    label = "Success rates simulated\nfrom the priors",
    hjust = 0.5,
    colour = simulated_blue,
    family = "Poppins"
  ) +
  annotate(
    "curve",
    x = 0.82,
    xend = observed + 0.02,
    y = 0.86 * tallest_bar,
    yend = 0.95 * tallest_bar,
    curvature = 0.3,
    arrow = arrow(length = unit(2, "mm"), type = "closed"),
    colour = observed_blue
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = 0.82,
    y = 0.76 * tallest_bar,
    label = str_glue(
      "Observed success rate\nin the sample ({scales::percent(observed, accuracy = 1)})"
    ),
    hjust = 0.5,
    colour = observed_blue,
    family = "Poppins"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(), limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(

    caption = socials

    axis.text.y = element_blank()

prior_check_plot

**Can the model recover known parameter values?** The prior predictive check above looks at whether the priors are sensible, but doesn't validate that the model can find true parameter values. If I simulate data using known parameters drawn from the priors and fit the model to the simulated data, do the model's estimates line up with the true values? Does each true value land in the middle half of the model's estimates about half the time, in the top tenth about a tenth of the time, etc? [Simulation-based calibration](https://arxiv.org/abs/1804.06788) checks this by fitting the model 200 times on different randomly simulated datasets. Because it's fitting the model 200 times, this part is computationally expensive (i.e., slow: about 15–20 min on my M5 MacBook Air).

In the chart below, each panel is one parameter. All but one of the lines stay inside the shaded bands (the third yards-needed curve pokes outside). The shaded regions are the area the line should stay in 95% of the time if the fitting works, so with 15 parameters one just poking out isn't a concern.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## ![R](/img/Rlogo.svg){height="25"}

```{r}
#| label: sbc-code
#| eval: false
#| code-summary: "R code · simulation-based calibration"
#| ref.label: [sbc, sbc-plot]
```

## ![Python](/img/python-logo-only.svg){height="30"}

```{python}
#| eval: false
#| code-summary: "Python code · simulation-based calibration"

rng = np.random.default_rng(20261007)
n_sims = 200
X_matrix = X.to_numpy()


# One simulated dataset: parameters drawn from the priors, then an outcome for
# every real play from those parameters
def simulate_dataset(rng):
    alpha = rng.normal(0, 1)
    beta = rng.normal(0, 0.35, X.width)
    log_odds = alpha + X_matrix @ beta
    return np.r_[alpha, beta], rng.binomial(1, expit(log_odds))


ranks, divergences, rhats = [], [], []
for _ in range(n_sims):
    truth, simulated_y = simulate_dataset(rng)
    # The same sampler settings as the real fit
    with build_model(X, simulated_y):
        sbc_fit = pm.sample(
            1000, tune=1000, chains=4, random_seed=rng, progressbar=False
        )

    posterior = sbc_fit.posterior
    draws = np.column_stack(
        [
            posterior["alpha"].values.ravel(),
            posterior["beta"].values.reshape(-1, X.width),
        ]
    )
    # Where each true value ranks among the draws, thinned to every 10th draw
    # so the ranks aren't distorted by autocorrelation
    ranks.append((draws[::10] < truth).mean(axis=0))
    divergences.append(int(sbc_fit.sample_stats["diverging"].sum()))
    convergence = az.summary(sbc_fit, var_names=["alpha", "beta"], kind="diagnostics")
    rhats.append(convergence["r_hat"].max())

pit = xr.Dataset(
    {"pit": (("chain", "draw", "parameter"), np.array(ranks)[None])},
    coords={"parameter": ["alpha", *X.columns]},
)
az.plot_ecdf_pit(xr.DataTree.from_dict({"prior_sbc": pit}))

print(
    f"{sum(divergences)} divergent transitions across {n_sims} simulated datasets; "
    f"largest R-hat {max(rhats):.3f}"
)
```

```{r}
#| label: sbc
#| cache: true
#| results: hide
#| include: false

sbc_data <- stan_data(plays, recipe)

# One simulated dataset: parameters drawn from the priors, then an outcome for
# every real play from those parameters
simulate_dataset <- function(data) {
  alpha <- rnorm(1, 0, 1)
  beta <- rnorm(data$K, 0, 0.35)
  log_odds <- alpha + drop(data$X %*% beta)

  list(
    variables = list(alpha = alpha, beta = beta),
    generated = modifyList(
      data,
      list(y = rbinom(data$N, 1, plogis(log_odds)))
    )
  )
}

set.seed(20261007)
datasets <- generate_datasets(
  SBC_generator_function(simulate_dataset, data = sbc_data),
  n_sims = 200
)

# The same sampler settings as the real fit, four simulations at a time
backend <- SBC_backend_cmdstan_sample(
  model,
  chains = 4,
  iter_warmup = 1000,
  iter_sampling = 1000
)

future::plan(future::multisession, workers = 4)
sbc <- compute_SBC(datasets, backend, keep_fits = FALSE)
future::plan(future::sequential)

# Name each weight after its feature (a curve has several weights)
weight_names <- tibble(
  variable = c("alpha", str_glue("beta[{seq_len(sbc_data$K)}]")),
  column = c("intercept", colnames(sbc_data$X))
) |>
  mutate(
    feature = str_remove(column, "_curve\\d+$"),
    curve = str_extract(column, "(?<=_curve)\\d+")
  ) |>
  left_join(dictionary |> select(feature, label), by = join_by(feature)) |>
  mutate(
    name = case_when(
      column == "intercept" ~ "Baseline",
      !is.na(curve) ~ str_glue("{label}, curve {curve}"),
      .default = label
    )
  )

## Fitting the model and checking the sampler (technical details)

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## ![R](/img/Rlogo.svg){height="25"}

```{r}
#| label: fit
#| code-summary: "R code · model fitting"
#| output: false

frames <- read_csv(
  file.path(data_url, "withheld_play_frames.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

fit <- model$sample(
  data = stan_data(plays, recipe, new = frames),
  seed = 2534,
  chains = 4,
  parallel_chains = 4,
  iter_warmup = 1000,
  iter_sampling = 1000,
  refresh = 0
)

# Every plausible set of weights, kept together as random variables
draws <- as_draws_rvars(fit$draws(c("alpha", "beta")))

inv_logit <- \(log_odds) 1 / (1 + exp(-log_odds))

predict_success <- function(plays) {
  log_odds <- draws$alpha +
    drop(
      design_matrix(plays, recipe) %**% draws$beta
    )
  inv_logit(log_odds)
}
```

## ![Python](/img/python-logo-only.svg){height="30"}

```{python}
#| eval: false
#| code-summary: "Python code · model fitting"

# Yards needed is a whole number in the first frames, so the column types are
# read from the whole file
frames = pl.read_csv(f"{DATA_URL}/withheld_play_frames.csv", infer_schema_length=None)

with build_model(X, y, design_matrix(frames, recipe)) as model:
    fit = pm.sample(1000, tune=1000, chains=4, random_seed=2534)
    # Pointwise log-likelihood, for leave-one-out cross-validation
    pm.compute_log_likelihood(fit)

# Every plausible set of weights: one row per posterior draw
alpha_draws = fit.posterior["alpha"].values.ravel()
beta_draws = fit.posterior["beta"].values.reshape(-1, X.width)


def predict_success(plays):
    """The probability of success for each play (columns), for every draw (rows)."""
    log_odds = (
        alpha_draws[:, None] + beta_draws @ design_matrix(plays, recipe).to_numpy().T
    )
    return expit(log_odds)
```
:::

**Did the fitting work?** Yes. These are the standard checks that the sampler explored properly, and that no single play pulls too hard on the fit.

## Posterior predictive check (technical details)

If the model is a good (albeit simplified) representation of reality, the outcomes it simulates should look like the ones observed in the real world. And they should do this across different subsets of interest (to show it's not just good in some areas but not others).

Here I use the model to simulate outcomes for every play in the training data, then compare the distribution of the simulated success rates with the actual success rates across downs and across yards needed for success. The observed rate is inside the model's expected plausible range in each scenario. The weakest spot is on plays needing 6 to 10 yards, where the model is a bit optimistic.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

The posterior predictive check shows that the model is able to accurately recover observed success rates across downs and across yards needed, but that's on plays the model has already seen. Its probabilities need to hold up on plays it hasn't seen to be practically useful.

## Did it cost predictive performance?

Did making the football concepts explicit and using a simpler, interpretable model cost much in predictive performance? No. 

It performed as well as the CNN, and a little better on every metric the CNN reports.

To make the comparison as fair as I could, I copied the reference eval by using the same 3,228 plays, the same five-fold [cross-validation](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fSytzGwwBVw) approach (stratified, seed 42), and the same definition of each metric.[^1] That's only possible because Lou published the plays, how they were split, and exactly how the model's performance was assessed 🙌 (many don't do this). Every prediction here was made by a version of the model that never saw that play (the code that does this is in the [appendix](#appendix)).

[^1]: Lou averaged four cross-validation runs with different folds and network training seeds. I ran one set of five folds. This model doesn't have the network's sensitivity to random starting weights, and the sampler checks suggest the MCMC noise is small.

```{r}

#| include: false

```{r}
#| output: false
#| code-summary: "R code · comparing model performance"

# Area under the precision-recall curve by the trapezoid rule, with an anchor
# at (recall 0, precision 1). This is sklearn's auc(recall, precision), the
# definition the reference CNN reports, and it gives a slightly different
# number from the step-wise "average precision".
pr_auc_trapz <- function(prob, y) {
  n_pos <- sum(y == 1L)
  if (n_pos == 0L || n_pos == length(y)) {
    return(NA_real_)
  }
  # A threshold includes every play with the same predicted probability.
  thresholds <- tibble(prob, y) |>
    summarise(n = n(), successes = sum(y == 1L), .by = prob) |>
    arrange(desc(prob)) |>
    mutate(
      true_positives = cumsum(successes),
      predicted_positives = cumsum(n)
    )
  precision <- c(1, thresholds$true_positives / thresholds$predicted_positives)
  recall <- c(0, thresholds$true_positives / n_pos)
  sum(diff(recall) * (precision[-length(precision)] + precision[-1]) / 2)
}

# Area under the ROC curve from the rank-sum identity.
roc_auc_fast <- function(prob, y) {
  n_pos <- sum(y == 1L)
  n_neg <- sum(y == 0L)
  if (n_pos == 0L || n_neg == 0L) {
    return(NA_real_)
  }
  ranks <- rank(prob, ties.method = "average")
  (sum(ranks[y == 1L]) - n_pos * (n_pos + 1) / 2) / (n_pos * n_neg)
}

# The four metrics the reference CNN reports, as a one-row tibble.
performance <- function(prob, y) {
  tibble(
    pr_auc = pr_auc_trapz(prob, y),
    roc_auc = roc_auc_fast(prob, y),
    accuracy = mean((prob >= 0.5) == (y == 1L)),
    brier = mean((prob - y)^2)
  )
}

# Predicted probabilities in equal-width bins against how often those plays
# succeeded. `lower` and `upper` are a 90% interval on the observed rate.
calibration_data <- function(prob_mean, y, n_bins = 10) {
  tibble(prob_mean = prob_mean, y = y) |>
    mutate(
      bin = cut(
        prob_mean,
        breaks = seq(0, 1, length.out = n_bins + 1),
        include.lowest = TRUE,
        labels = FALSE
      )
    ) |>
    summarise(
      n = n(),
      n_success = sum(y),
      mean_pred = mean(prob_mean),
      mean_obs = mean(y),
      lower = qbeta(0.05, n_success + 0.5, n - n_success + 0.5),
      upper = qbeta(0.95, n_success + 0.5, n - n_success + 0.5),
      .by = bin
    ) |>
    arrange(bin)
}

# `reference` holds the cross-validated predictions (the code is in the
# appendix)

model_performance <- performance(reference$p_mean, reference$success)

success_rate <- mean(reference$success)

comparison <- bind_rows(
  # Conventional no-skill PR reference; constant mean predictions for the

```{python}
#| eval: false
#| code-summary: "Python code · comparing model performance"


def pr_auc_trapz(prob, y):
    """Area under the precision-recall curve by the trapezoid rule.

    Anchored at (recall 0, precision 1). This is sklearn's auc(recall, precision),
    the definition the reference CNN reports, and it gives a slightly different
    number from the step-wise "average precision".
    """
    n_pos = (y == 1).sum()
    if n_pos in (0, len(y)):
        return np.nan
    # A threshold includes every play with the same predicted probability
    thresholds = (
        pl.DataFrame({"prob": prob, "y": y})
        .group_by("prob")
        .agg(n=pl.len(), successes=(pl.col("y") == 1).sum())
        .sort("prob", descending=True)
        .with_columns(
            true_positives=pl.col("successes").cum_sum(),
            predicted_positives=pl.col("n").cum_sum(),
        )
    )
    true_positives = thresholds["true_positives"].to_numpy()
    precision = np.r_[1, true_positives / thresholds["predicted_positives"].to_numpy()]
    recall = np.r_[0, true_positives / n_pos]
    return np.trapezoid(precision, recall)


def roc_auc_fast(prob, y):
    """Area under the ROC curve from the rank-sum identity."""
    n_pos = (y == 1).sum()
    n_neg = (y == 0).sum()
    if n_pos == 0 or n_neg == 0:
        return np.nan
    ranks = stats.rankdata(prob)
    return (ranks[y == 1].sum() - n_pos * (n_pos + 1) / 2) / (n_pos * n_neg)


def performance(prob, y):
    """The four metrics the reference CNN reports."""
    return {
        "pr_auc": pr_auc_trapz(prob, y),
        "roc_auc": roc_auc_fast(prob, y),
        "accuracy": np.mean((prob >= 0.5) == (y == 1)),
        "brier": np.mean((prob - y) ** 2),
    }


def calibration_data(prob_mean, y, n_bins=10):
    """Predicted probabilities in equal-width bins against how often those plays
    succeeded. `lower` and `upper` are a 90% interval on the observed rate."""
    calibration = (
        pl.DataFrame({"prob_mean": prob_mean, "y": y})
        .with_columns(
            bin=pl.col("prob_mean").cut(np.linspace(0, 1, n_bins + 1)[1:-1].tolist())
        )
        .group_by("bin")
        .agg(
            n=pl.len(),
            n_success=pl.col("y").sum(),
            mean_pred=pl.col("prob_mean").mean(),
            mean_obs=pl.col("y").mean(),
        )
        .sort("mean_pred")
    )
    a = calibration["n_success"] + 0.5
    b = calibration["n"] - calibration["n_success"] + 0.5
    return calibration.with_columns(
        lower=pl.Series(stats.beta.ppf(0.05, a, b)),
        upper=pl.Series(stats.beta.ppf(0.95, a, b)),
    )


# `reference` holds the cross-validated predictions (the code is in the
# appendix)
reference_p = reference["p_mean"].to_numpy()
reference_y = reference["success"].to_numpy()

model_performance = performance(reference_p, reference_y)

success_rate = reference_y.mean()

comparison = pl.DataFrame(
    [
        # Conventional no-skill PR reference; constant mean predictions for the
        # accuracy and Brier baselines
        {
            "model": "No-skill baseline",
            "pr_auc": success_rate,
            "roc_auc": 0.5,
            "accuracy": np.mean((success_rate >= 0.5) == (reference_y == 1)),
            "brier": np.mean((success_rate - reference_y) ** 2),
        },
        # Published by the reference project, averaged over four training runs
        {
            "model": "Reference CNN",
            "pr_auc": 0.7929,
            "roc_auc": 0.7314,
            "accuracy": 0.6808,
            "brier": 0.2026,
        },
        {"model": "This model", **model_performance},
    ]
)

(
    GT(comparison)
    .fmt_number(columns=["pr_auc", "roc_auc", "accuracy", "brier"], decimals=3)
    .cols_label(
        model="",
        pr_auc="PR-AUC",
        roc_auc="ROC-AUC",
        accuracy="Accuracy",
        brier="Brier score*",
    )
    .tab_source_note("* Lower is better. Higher is better for the other scores.")
)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## What the four scores mean

-   **PR-AUC** (area under the precision-recall curve): how well a model ranks successful plays above unsuccessful ones, weighted towards the plays it rates highest. 1 is perfect. The no-skill reference is the overall success rate (`r scales::number(comparison$pr_auc[1], accuracy = 0.01)`).
-   **ROC-AUC** (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve): the chance that a randomly picked successful play is rated higher than a randomly picked unsuccessful one. 0.5 is a coin flip and 1 is perfect.
-   **Accuracy**: the share of plays called correctly, counting anything rated 50% or more as a call of success.
-   **Brier score**: the average squared gap between the predicted probability and what happened (1 for a successful play, 0 otherwise). It rewards probabilities that are confident and right. Lower is better, and always guessing the average scores `r scales::number(comparison$brier[1], accuracy = 0.01)`.
:::

The headline metric in the CNN post is [PR-AUC](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4jRBRDbJemM&t=824s). The logistic regression model scores **`r scales::number(model_performance$pr_auc, accuracy = 0.001)`** against the CNN's **0.793**. This doesn't mean "regression beats neural networks" (because often it won't), but on this problem I didn't have to give up any predictive ability to get a model that is more transparent about what contributes to a given prediction.

This compares the two approaches as a whole. My model also includes receiver depth relative to the line of scrimmage, which wasn't included in the CNN's inputs. Some of the improvement is from that extra context.

### Can you believe the probabilities?

If a model says 70% probability of success, plays like that should succeed about 70% of the time. This characteristic is called calibration. A coach reviewing plays rated 70% should expect roughly seven in ten of them to have worked. If plays rated 70% keep succeeding only about half the time across lots of plays, the model is poorly calibrated.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## What the model says

Yards needed for a successful play is associated with the largest change in estimated success probability, followed by receiver depth.

Here I look at how each of the six football concepts (rather than the nine individual features) is associated with success. For each concept, I compare the tenth of plays with the least of it to the tenth with the most, holding everything else at average. For example, going from the plays needing the fewest yards to those needing the most lowers the estimated probability of success by about 72 percentage points. Concepts associated with a higher probability of success sit to the right of zero, and those associated with a lower one sit to the left.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## ![R](/img/Rlogo.svg){height="25"}

```{r}
#| output: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5.6

# Which feature each column of the design matrix belongs to (curve has
# several columns)
training_matrix <- design_matrix(plays, recipe)
column_feature <- str_remove(colnames(training_matrix), "_curve\\d+$")

# The football ideas are the feature groups
ideas <- dictionary |>
  mutate(idea = group)

# Each idea's direction is set by one of its features
directions <- tribble(
  ~idea                       , ~headline                   , ~direction                                ,
  "What the play needs"       , "yards_needed"              , "More yards needed"                       ,
  "How deep the receiver is"  , "receiver_depth"            , "Receiver further downfield"              ,
  "Space around the receiver" , "room_beyond_nearest"       , "More room ahead"                         ,
  "Help from blockers"        , "nearest_blocker_advantage" , "Nearest defender further from a blocker" ,
  "Shape of the defence"      , "def_y_spread"              , "Wider defence"                           ,
  "Who is arriving"           , "mean_top3_closing_speed"   , "Nearest three closing faster"
)

# For one idea: what its features add to the log-odds on every real play, then
# the change in probability from the tenth of plays with the least of its
# headline feature to the tenth with the most, on an otherwise average play
idea_swing <- function(this_idea, headline) {
  columns <- column_feature %in% ideas$feature[ideas$idea == this_idea]
  contribution <- (training_matrix[, columns, drop = FALSE] %**%
    draws$beta[columns])[, 1]
  value <- plays[[headline]]
  least <- value <= quantile(value, 0.1)
  most <- value >= quantile(value, 0.9)

  (inv_logit(draws$alpha + rvar_mean(contribution[most])) -
    inv_logit(draws$alpha + rvar_mean(contribution[least]))) *
    100
}

signed_points <- scales::label_number(
  accuracy = 1,
  style_positive = "plus",
  style_negative = "minus"
)

leans_on <- ideas |>
  distinct(idea) |>
  inner_join(directions, by = join_by(idea), unmatched = "error") |>
  mutate(
    swing = map2(idea, headline, idea_swing) |> list_c(),
    estimate = mean(swing),
    label = str_glue(
      "{idea}<br><span style='font-size:10pt; color:#666666;'>{direction}</span>"
    ),
    label = fct_reorder(label, abs(estimate))
  )

# The annotations go on the idea that pushes up most, where there is room
annotated <- leans_on |> slice_max(estimate)
annotated_row <- as.numeric(annotated$label)
annotated_upper <- quantile(annotated$swing, 0.99)

effects_plot <- leans_on |>
  ggplot(aes(y = label, xdist = swing)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey70") +
  stat_slab(fill = pale_navy, height = 0.8) +
  stat_spike(at = "mean", size = 0, colour = navy, height = 0.8) +
  geom_text(
    aes(x = estimate, y = label, label = signed_points(estimate)),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    vjust = 1.4,
    colour = navy,
    family = "Poppins",
    size = 3.2
  ) +
  scale_thickness_shared() +
  annotate(
    "curve",
    x = annotated$estimate + 9,
    xend = annotated$estimate + 0.4,
    y = annotated_row + 0.9,
    yend = annotated_row + 0.68,
    curvature = 0.3,
    arrow = arrow(length = unit(2, "mm"), type = "closed"),
    colour = navy
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = annotated$estimate + 9.5,
    y = annotated_row + 0.9,
    label = "Average estimated change",
    hjust = 0,
    colour = navy,
    family = "Poppins",
    size = 3.6
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = annotated_upper + 4,
    y = annotated_row + 0.2,
    label = "Less likely,\nbut possible",
    hjust = 0,
    lineheight = 0.9,
    # Darker than the slab's fill so the text stays readable
    colour = "#5576A6",
    family = "Poppins",
    size = 3.6
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    # Zero in the middle, so pushes down and up read the same way
    limits = \(range) c(-1, 1) * max(abs(range)),
    expand = expansion(mult = 0.05),
    breaks = scales::breaks_width(25),
    labels = scales::label_number(
      suffix = " pts",
      style_positive = "plus",
      style_negative = "minus"
    )
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  labs(
    title = "Yards needed matters most, then how deep the receiver is",
    subtitle = "Change in the probability of success (percentage points) from the tenth of plays\nwith the least of each to the tenth with the most, everything else average",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    caption = socials
  ) +
  theme(
    axis.text.y = element_markdown(lineheight = 1.2),
    # Room for the annotation, which sits right of the largest push up
    plot.margin = margin_part(r = 60)
  )

effects_plot

```{python}
#| eval: false

# Which feature each column of the design matrix belongs to (a curve has
# several columns)
training_matrix = design_matrix(plays, recipe)
column_feature = np.array(
    [column.split("_curve")[0] for column in training_matrix.columns]
)

# The football ideas are the feature groups
ideas = dictionary.select("feature", idea="group")

# Each idea's direction is set by one of its features
directions = pl.DataFrame(
    {
        "idea": [
            "What the play needs",
            "How deep the receiver is",
            "Space around the receiver",
            "Help from blockers",
            "Shape of the defence",
            "Who is arriving",
        ],
        "headline": [
            "yards_needed",
            "receiver_depth",
            "room_beyond_nearest",
            "nearest_blocker_advantage",
            "def_y_spread",
            "mean_top3_closing_speed",
        ],
        "direction": [
            "More yards needed",
            "Receiver further downfield",
            "More room ahead",
            "Nearest defender further from a blocker",
            "Wider defence",
            "Nearest three closing faster",
        ],
    }
)


def idea_swing(idea, headline):
    """What one idea's features add to the log-odds on every real play, then the
    change in probability (percentage points) from the tenth of plays with the
    least of its headline feature to the tenth with the most, on an otherwise
    average play. One value per posterior draw."""
    features = ideas.filter(pl.col("idea") == idea)["feature"]
    columns = np.isin(column_feature, features)
    # Plays in rows, draws in columns
    contribution = training_matrix.to_numpy()[:, columns] @ beta_draws[:, columns].T
    value = plays[headline].to_numpy()
    least = value <= np.quantile(value, 0.1)
    most = value >= np.quantile(value, 0.9)

    return (
        expit(alpha_draws + contribution[most].mean(axis=0))
        - expit(alpha_draws + contribution[least].mean(axis=0))
    ) * 100


def interval_plot(ax, draws):
    """The mean and a 90% interval for each set of draws, one row per label."""
    means = np.array([values.mean() for values in draws.values()])
    lower, upper = np.percentile(np.array(list(draws.values())), [5, 95], axis=1)
    rows = np.arange(len(draws))
    ax.axvline(0, color="grey", linewidth=0.8)
    ax.errorbar(means, rows, xerr=[means - lower, upper - means], fmt="o", color=NAVY)
    ax.set_yticks(rows, labels=list(draws))


swings = {
    idea: idea_swing(idea, headline)
    for idea, headline in directions.select("idea", "headline").iter_rows()
}

leans_on = directions.with_columns(
    estimate=pl.Series([swings[idea].mean() for idea in directions["idea"]])
).sort(pl.col("estimate").abs())

print(leans_on.select("idea", "direction", "estimate"))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5))
interval_plot(ax, {idea: swings[idea] for idea in leans_on["idea"]})
ax.set_xlabel("Change in the probability of success (percentage points)")
ax.set_title("Yards needed matters most, then how deep the receiver is", loc="left")
fig.tight_layout()

#| fig-alt: "Diagram with four boxes and arrows. 'The play at the throw' points to 'A successful play', with the label 'Association the model learns'. A dashed box, 'What the features can't see', points to the play at the throw, to a successful play and to 'The QB throws and it's caught'. The play at the throw also points to 'The QB throws and it's caught', which is shaded because every play in the data is a completed pass."
dag_plot
```

First, things the features don't contain (e.g., the coverage, how good the receiver is, whether the throwing lane is open, etc) impact both the space around a receiver and how the play ends. Part of the reason why plays with space around the receiver succeed is what tends to come with the space, like a good receiver or a beaten coverage. That's confounding and is why the model's estimates can't be interpreted as unbiased causal effects.

Second, every play here is one where the QB decided to throw and the pass was caught. Both depend partly on the space around the receiver and partly on those same unseen things. A tightly covered receiver might only get the ball when it's a favourable matchup, and the throws into tight coverage that were broken up or intercepted aren't in the data at all. Each of these makes tight coverage look less costly to the model than it really is. This is selection bias, and it also stops the model's estimates from being read as causal effects.

The question a coach actually cares about ("what might happen if we change this?") is a causal one and needs a different research design and stronger assumptions to answer. What this model and chart *are* good for is arguing with. For example, a coach might challenge the model by saying:

> "Defensive width barely matters? That can't be right."

Maybe width matters through the coverage it signals, which the features can't see? Maybe a standard deviation is the wrong way to measure it? That's a conversation and opportunity to iterate that's much harder to have with predictions from a neural network.
:::

## The model on real plays

The model wasn't trained on the three plays in the videos, and they have tracking data for every tenth of a second from the snap to the throw. So here I use the model to estimate, at every frame: **if the ball was thrown now and caught, what's the probability of a successful play?**

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## ![R](/img/Rlogo.svg){height="25"}

```{r}
#| output: false

# One random variable per frame: the model's probability at that moment
frames <- frames |>
  mutate(probability = as_draws_rvars(fit$draws("p_new"))$p_new)

featured <- tribble(
  ~game_id   , ~play_id , ~play                   , ~game                       ,
  2022100901 ,     2020 , "Pickett to Harris"     , "Steelers @ Bills, 2022"    ,
  2022102700 ,     2820 , "Jackson to Robinson"   , "Ravens @ Buccaneers, 2022" ,
  2021091212 ,      611 , "Bridgewater to Gordon" , "Broncos @ Giants, 2021"
)

# The reading when the ball leaves the passer's hand. Like the videos, it is
# averaged over the last three frames (0.3 seconds).
at_release <- frames |>
  inner_join(featured, by = join_by(game_id, play_id)) |>
  arrange(game_id, play_id, frame_idx) |>
  summarise(
    reading = rvar_mean(tail(probability, 3)),
    .by = c(
      game_id,
      play_id,
      play,
      game,
      down,
      yards_to_go,
      yards_gained,
      success
    )
  ) |>
  mutate(
    estimate = mean(reading),
    lower = quantile(reading, 0.05)[1, ],
    upper = quantile(reading, 0.95)[1, ]
  )

percent <- scales::label_percent(accuracy = 1)
reading_of <- function(id) {
  at_release |>
    filter(play_id == id) |>
    str_glue_data(
      "{percent(estimate)} (90% credible interval {percent(lower)} to {percent(upper)})"
    )
}

featured_table <- at_release |>
  arrange(match(play_id, featured$play_id)) |>
  mutate(
    play = str_glue(
      "<div style='font-weight:600;'>{play}</div>",
      "<div style='font-size:12px; color:#666666;'>{game}</div>"
    ),
    situation = str_glue("{ordinal[down]} & {yards_to_go}"),
    reading = probability_pill(estimate, percent(estimate)),
    interval = str_glue("{percent(lower)} to {percent(upper)}"),
    gained = str_glue(
      "{yards_gained} {if_else(yards_gained == 1, 'yard', 'yards')}"
    ),
    result = if_else(
      success,
      pill("Successful", "#166534", "#DCFCE7"),
      pill("Not successful", "#475569", "#E8ECF1")
    ),
    .keep = "none"
  ) |>
  gt() |>
  post_table() |>
  fmt_markdown(columns = c(play, reading, result)) |>
  cols_align(align = "left", columns = c(play, situation)) |>
  cols_align(align = "center", columns = c(reading, result)) |>
  cols_label(
    play = "Play",
    situation = "Situation",
    reading = "Model",
    interval = "90% interval",
    gained = "Gained",
    result = "Result"
  ) |>
  tab_spanner(label = "At the throw", columns = c(reading, interval)) |>
  tab_spanner(label = "What happened", columns = c(gained, result)) |>
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(color = "grey40"),
    locations = cells_body(columns = interval)
  )

#| eval: false

# One row per posterior draw, one column per frame: the model's probability at
# that moment
frame_probabilities = fit.posterior["p_new"].values.reshape(-1, frames.height)
frames = frames.with_row_index("frame_row")

featured = pl.DataFrame(
    {
        "game_id": [2022100901, 2022102700, 2021091212],
        "play_id": [2020, 2820, 611],
        "play": ["Pickett to Harris", "Jackson to Robinson", "Bridgewater to Gordon"],
        "game": [
            "Steelers @ Bills, 2022",
            "Ravens @ Buccaneers, 2022",
            "Broncos @ Giants, 2021",
        ],
    }
)


def reading_at_release(game_id, play_id):
    """The reading when the ball leaves the passer's hand. Like the videos, it's
    averaged over the last three frames (0.3 seconds). One value per draw."""
    rows = (
        frames.filter(pl.col("game_id") == game_id, pl.col("play_id") == play_id)
        .sort("frame_idx")
        .tail(3)["frame_row"]
    )
    return frame_probabilities[:, rows.to_numpy()].mean(axis=1)


readings = {
    play_id: reading_at_release(game_id, play_id)
    for game_id, play_id in featured.select("game_id", "play_id").iter_rows()
}

at_release = featured.join(
    frames.group_by("game_id", "play_id").agg(
        pl.col("down", "yards_to_go", "yards_gained", "success").last()
    ),
    on=["game_id", "play_id"],
    maintain_order="left",
).with_columns(
    estimate=pl.Series([readings[i].mean() for i in featured["play_id"]]),
    lower=pl.Series([np.quantile(readings[i], 0.05) for i in featured["play_id"]]),
    upper=pl.Series([np.quantile(readings[i], 0.95) for i in featured["play_id"]]),
)

ORDINAL = {1: "1st", 2: "2nd", 3: "3rd", 4: "4th"}

(
    GT(
        at_release.select(
            "play",
            "game",
            situation=pl.format(
                "{} & {}", pl.col("down").replace_strict(ORDINAL), pl.col("yards_to_go")
            ),
            model="estimate",
            lower="lower",
            upper="upper",
            gained="yards_gained",
            result=pl.when("success")
            .then(pl.lit("Successful"))
            .otherwise(pl.lit("Not successful")),
        )
    )
    .fmt_percent(columns=["model", "lower", "upper"], decimals=0)
    .tab_spanner("At the throw (90% interval)", columns=["model", "lower", "upper"])
    .tab_spanner("What happened", columns=["gained", "result"])
)

It needs 9 yards (more than most plays in the sample), and the receiver is behind the line of scrimmage when the ball's thrown. Those are the two features that move the estimate most, and both are unfavourable here, so a low probability is expected. But 21% doesn't mean "this won't work". It means plays like this work about 1 time in 5 (with a [well calibrated](#can-you-believe-the-probabilities) model like this one). During cross-validation, the model rated `r sum(reference$p_mean > 0.15 & reference$p_mean <= 0.25)` plays between 15% and 25%, and `r percent(mean(reference$success[reference$p_mean > 0.15 & reference$p_mean <= 0.25]))` of them succeeded.

::: callout-tip
## You can't judge a probability on one play

You judge it on whether the 20%s happen about 20% of the time across lots of plays. And the credible interval tells you how certain the model is about that 20% given the plays it learned from.
:::

### Why the number moves

In the [first video at the top](#opening-play) (Broncos @ Giants), the probability of success climbs from about 40% at the snap to over 80%, then drops back to `r percent(at_release$estimate[at_release$play_id == 611])` by the time Teddy Bridgewater throws it for a 1-yard gain.

Because the model is built from features describing football concepts, I can inspect why the number moved. I split the play into (1) from the snap to the peak, and (2) from the peak to the throw. For each period, I attribute the change in the model's prediction to the football concepts to see which contributed most. Yards needed doesn't change during a play, so it's not shown.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## ![R](/img/Rlogo.svg){height="25"}

```{r}
#| output: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5.5

play_611 <- frames |>
  filter(play_id == 611) |>
  arrange(frame_idx)

snap <- play_611 |> slice_head(n = 1)
peak <- play_611 |> slice_max(mean(probability), n = 1)
release <- play_611 |> slice_tail(n = 1)

# Exact grouped Shapley values: average each concept's contribution over all
# possible orders of changing the concepts from the earlier to the later frame.
# Subset weights give the same average without evaluating every permutation.
# This explains the model's prediction, not the effect of changing a real play.
what_moved <- function(earlier, later) {
  idea_names <- unique(ideas$idea)
  n_ideas <- length(idea_names)
  subsets <- expand_grid(
    !!!set_names(
      rep(list(c(FALSE, TRUE)), n_ideas),
      idea_names
    )
  )

  probabilities <- map(seq_len(nrow(subsets)), \(row) {
    changed_ideas <- idea_names[as.logical(subsets[row, ])]
    changed_features <- ideas$feature[ideas$idea %in% changed_ideas]
    hybrid <- earlier |>
      mutate(across(all_of(changed_features), \(value) later[[cur_column()]]))
    predict_success(hybrid)
  })

  changes <- map(idea_names, \(this_idea) {
    without <- which(!subsets[[this_idea]])
    contributions <- map(without, \(row) {
      with_idea <- subsets[row, ]
      with_idea[[this_idea]] <- TRUE
      matching_row <- which(map_lgl(seq_len(nrow(subsets)), \(candidate) {
        identical(subsets[candidate, ], with_idea)
      }))
      n_before <- sum(as.logical(subsets[row, ]))
      weight <- 1 / (n_ideas * choose(n_ideas - 1, n_before))
      (probabilities[[matching_row]] - probabilities[[row]]) * weight * 100
    })
    reduce(contributions, `+`)
  })

  tibble(idea = idea_names, change = list_c(changes))
}

moves <- bind_rows(
  `From the snap to the peak` = what_moved(snap, peak),
  `From the peak to the throw` = what_moved(peak, release),
  .id = "stage"
) |>
  filter_out(idea == "What the play needs") |>
  mutate(
    stage = fct_inorder(stage),
    # The same order as the effects chart
    idea = factor(
      idea,
      levels = leans_on |> arrange(abs(estimate)) |> pull(idea)
    )
  )

# The whole change at each stage, for the panel headings
total_change <- function(earlier, later) {
  mean(predict_success(later) - predict_success(earlier)) * 100
}

stage_labels <- c(
  `From the snap to the peak` = str_glue(
    "From the snap to the peak: {signed_points(total_change(snap, peak))} pts"
  ),
  `From the peak to the throw` = str_glue(
    "From the peak to the throw: {signed_points(total_change(peak, release))} pts"
  )
)

what_moved_plot <- moves |>
  mutate(estimate = mean(change)) |>
  ggplot(aes(y = idea, xdist = change)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey70") +
  # Each slab to its own height: some changes are so certain that, on a shared
  # scale, they would flatten the rest
  stat_slab(fill = pale_navy, height = 0.8, normalize = "xy") +
  stat_spike(
    at = "mean",
    size = 0,
    colour = navy,
    height = 0.8,
    normalize = "xy"
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(x = estimate, y = idea, label = signed_points(estimate)),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    vjust = 1.4,
    colour = navy,
    family = "Poppins",
    size = 3.2
  ) +
  facet_wrap(vars(stage), labeller = as_labeller(stage_labels)) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    limits = \(range) c(-1, 1) * max(abs(range)),
    breaks = c(-30, 0, 30),
    labels = scales::label_number(
      suffix = " pts",
      style_positive = "plus",
      style_negative = "minus"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Receiver got through the linemen, then a defender closes in",
    subtitle = "Contribution to the change in predicted success probability (percentage points)",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    caption = socials
  ) +
  theme(
    strip.text = element_text(hjust = 0),
    panel.spacing.x = unit(2, "lines")
  )

what_moved_plot
```

```{python}
#| eval: false

play_611 = frames.filter(pl.col("play_id") == 611).sort("frame_idx")
mean_probability = frame_probabilities[:, play_611["frame_row"].to_numpy()].mean(axis=0)

snap = play_611.head(1)
peak = play_611.slice(int(mean_probability.argmax()), 1)
release = play_611.tail(1)


def what_moved(earlier, later):
    """Exact grouped Shapley values: each concept's contribution averaged over
    all possible orders of changing the concepts from the earlier to the later
    frame. Subset weights give the same average without evaluating every
    permutation. This explains the model's prediction, not the effect of
    changing a real play. One value per draw, in percentage points."""
    idea_names = ideas["idea"].unique(maintain_order=True).to_list()
    n_ideas = len(idea_names)
    subsets = list(itertools.product([False, True], repeat=n_ideas))

    probabilities = {}
    for subset in subsets:
        changed = [idea for idea, is_changed in zip(idea_names, subset) if is_changed]
        changed_features = ideas.filter(pl.col("idea").is_in(changed))[
            "feature"
        ].to_list()
        hybrid = earlier.with_columns(later.select(changed_features).get_columns())
        probabilities[subset] = predict_success(hybrid)[:, 0]

    changes = {}
    for i, idea in enumerate(idea_names):
        change = 0
        for subset in subsets:
            if subset[i]:
                continue
            with_idea = subset[:i] + (True,) + subset[i + 1 :]
            weight = 1 / (n_ideas * math.comb(n_ideas - 1, sum(subset)))
            change = (
                change
                + (probabilities[with_idea] - probabilities[subset]) * weight * 100
            )
        changes[idea] = change

    return changes


def total_change(earlier, later):
    """The whole change in the probability of success, in percentage points."""
    return (predict_success(later) - predict_success(earlier)).mean() * 100


stages = {
    "From the snap to the peak": (snap, peak),
    "From the peak to the throw": (peak, release),
}
# Yards needed doesn't change during a play. The same order as the effects chart
shown_ideas = [idea for idea in leans_on["idea"] if idea != "What the play needs"]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 5), sharey=True)
for ax, (stage, (earlier, later)) in zip(axes, stages.items()):
    changes = what_moved(earlier, later)
    interval_plot(ax, {idea: changes[idea] for idea in shown_ideas})
    ax.set_title(f"{stage}: {total_change(earlier, later):+.0f} pts", loc="left")
    print(
        f"{stage}: "
        + ", ".join(f"{idea} {changes[idea].mean():+.1f}" for idea in shown_ideas)
    )
fig.supxlabel(
    "Contribution to the change in predicted success probability (percentage points)"
)
fig.tight_layout()

From the snap to the peak the probability rises about 50 points, mostly from receiver depth, contributing 23 points, then space around the receiver and who is arriving, about 14 and 13. From the peak to the throw it falls about 50 points, mostly from help from blockers, contributing minus 27 points, then who is arriving, minus 15, and space around the receiver, minus 10. The other concepts contribute little."
