The number rises because Melvin Gordon works through the defensive linemen and up to the line of scrimmage with room on either side. It falls because the nearest defender closes in with no nearby blockers.

That explains the change in football terms. Experts can hold it up against the film and challenge it until it's refined enough to trust.

## The limits

Every play the model learned from is a moment a QB chose to throw. The earlier frames in the videos are moments the QB chose not to, probably for reasons the features can't see (the dashed box in the [DAG above](#not-instructions)). So the number could be a bit off before the throw, and its interval doesn't widen to warn you. Bridgewater might have held on to the ball through the peak above 80% because of something the model can't see. 

To summarise the limitations of my model (and of any model of this data, short of assumptions I don't think hold):

-   **It isn't causal.** It describes what tends to go with success ([these are not instructions](#not-instructions)). It can't tell you what would happen if a player did something different.
-   **It only knows about completed passes.** It never saw a pass that was dropped, missed its target, intercepted, blocked, etc. So its number assumes the catch is made and risky throws look better than they are.
-   **It knows nothing about the actual throw.** The features describe the space around the receiver, not the path the ball has to travel. A moment it rates highly might have a defensive lineman standing in the throwing lane with hands up.
-   **Before the throw, it's answering a different question.** It learned from moments quarterbacks chose to throw, not moments they held on. [See above](#not-instructions).
-   **It's 3,228 completed short passes** from the first half of two seasons.

## The wrap

I wanted to see whether compressing the information from complex, high-dimensional tracking inputs into features representing football concepts would cost much in predictive performance. In this case it didn't. 

That doesn't mean neural networks are the wrong tool. If nobody knows how to describe what matters, letting a flexible model find patterns in the raw data is a good approach, and it's probably a sensible place to start with tracking data. What I found is that this outcome could be described well by nine features covering six football concepts. Once that's true, the simple model is the easier one to inspect, question, and trust.

It also shows that football knowledge can go *into* a model, not just come out of it. Yards needed, the feature most strongly associated with success, is just the success rule applied to down and distance. The CNN had to learn that rule; I could just tell the model.

It could be applied practically in film review with players. Why does the model like one situation more than another? Does that match what they see? If not, what has it missed? It'd also be interesting to see which players consistently succeed more or less often than the model expects (implications on player evaluation and scouting). For real use though, I'd want a version trained on every throw (incompletions and interceptions included), not just the completed ones, and ideally one that also models when quarterbacks choose to throw.

::: callout-note

You'll need R with the packages loaded at the top of the post (dplyr ≥ 1.2.0; [`SBC`](https://github.com/hyunjimoon/SBC) installs from GitHub), [my `mitchhenderson` package](https://github.com/mitchhenderson/mitchhenderson-R-package) for the chart captions (`remotes::install_github("mitchhenderson/mitchhenderson-R-package")`), [CmdStan](https://mc-stan.org/cmdstanr/articles/cmdstanr.html) and the Poppins font. The videos aren't included because they contain broadcast footage.
-   **The Python version** uses the same files. You'll need [Polars](https://pola.rs/), [PyMC](https://www.pymc.io/), [ArviZ](https://www.arviz.org/), [formulaic](https://matthewwardrop.github.io/formulaic/), SciPy, matplotlib, [great_tables](https://posit-dev.github.io/great-tables/) and [`rdata`](https://rdata.readthedocs.io/) (to read the example play's `.rds` file). I ran it with PyMC 6.3, ArviZ 1.3 and Polars 2.0.

## Appendix {#appendix}

### Cross-validation

Every prediction in the comparison was made by a model that never saw that play. The plays are split into five folds, and the model is fitted on four and predicts the fifth, once for each fold. The folds are made the same way as the reference project's (stratified five-fold, seed 42), and centres, scales and spline knots are learned from the four training folds only.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## ![R](/img/Rlogo.svg){height="25"}

```{r}
#| label: cross-validation
#| eval: false
#| code-summary: "R code · cross-validation"

# Fit on every fold but one and predict the plays in the fold left out
predict_fold <- function(held_out) {
  train <- plays |> filter(fold != held_out)
  test <- plays |> filter(fold == held_out)

  fold_fit <- model$sample(
    data = stan_data(train, design_recipe(train, final_features), new = test),
    seed = 2534,
    chains = 4,
    parallel_chains = 4,
    iter_warmup = 1000,
    iter_sampling = 1000,
    refresh = 0
  )

  sampler <- fold_fit$diagnostic_summary(quiet = TRUE)
  convergence <- fold_fit$draws(c("alpha", "beta")) |>
    summarise_draws(rhat, ess_bulk, ess_tail)
  if (
    sum(sampler$num_divergent) > 0 ||
      max(convergence$rhat) >= 1.01 ||
      min(convergence$ess_bulk, convergence$ess_tail) <= 400
  ) {
    cli::cli_abort("Fold {held_out} failed its checks.")
  }

  probability <- as_draws_rvars(fold_fit$draws("p_new"))$p_new

  test |>
    mutate(
      game_id,
      play_id,
      success,
      p_mean = mean(probability)
    )
}

# A prediction for every play, each from the model that left its fold out
reference <- map(1:5, predict_fold) |>
  list_rbind()
```

## ![Python](/img/python-logo-only.svg){height="30"}

```{python}
#| eval: false
#| code-summary: "Python code · cross-validation"


def predict_fold(held_out):
    """Fit on every fold but one and predict the plays in the fold left out."""
    train = plays.filter(pl.col("fold") != held_out)
    test = plays.filter(pl.col("fold") == held_out)
    fold_recipe = design_recipe(train, final_features)

    with build_model(
        design_matrix(train, fold_recipe),
        train["success"].to_numpy(),
        design_matrix(test, fold_recipe),
    ):
        fold_fit = pm.sample(
            1000, tune=1000, chains=4, random_seed=2534, progressbar=False
        )

    convergence = az.summary(fold_fit, var_names=["alpha", "beta"], kind="diagnostics")
    if (
        fold_fit.sample_stats["diverging"].sum() > 0
        or convergence["r_hat"].max() >= 1.01
        or min(convergence["ess_bulk"].min(), convergence["ess_tail"].min()) <= 400
    ):
        raise RuntimeError(f"Fold {held_out} failed its checks.")

    return test.with_columns(
        p_mean=fold_fit.posterior["p_new"].mean(("chain", "draw")).values
    )


# A prediction for every play, each from the model that left its fold out
reference = pl.concat([predict_fold(fold) for fold in range(1, 6)])
```

socials <- mitchhenderson::social_caption(

  theme_classic(base_size = 14, base_family = "Poppins") +
    theme(
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 12, colour = "grey40"),
      axis.title.x = element_text(size = 12, colour = "grey40"),
      axis.title.y = element_text(size = 12, colour = "grey40"),
      # Set the social caption apart from the axis title above it. Its size
      # is set for each chart below.
      plot.caption = element_markdown(
        colour = "grey50",
        margin = margin(t = 16)
      ),
      axis.ticks = element_blank(),
      axis.line = element_line(colour = "grey50"),
      strip.background = element_blank(),
      strip.text = element_text(hjust = 0, face = "bold"),
      plot.title.position = "plot"
    )
)

# bayesplot draws its checks in the same blues as everything else
color_scheme_set(c(
  "#E3EAF4",
  pale_navy,
  "#8FA9CB",
  "#5B80B3",
  navy,
  "#0D3566"
))

bayesplot_theme_set(theme_get())

# Charts are drawn at different widths and scaled to fit the page, so a
# caption with a fixed point size shows at a different size on each. Sizing it
# from the chart's width makes every caption show at the tables' 13px when the
# chart fills the 682px text column.
caption_size <- function(fig_width = knitr::opts_current$get("fig.width")) {
  13 * 0.75 * fig_width * 96 / 682
}

knitr::opts_hooks$set(fig.width = function(options) {
  size <- caption_size(options$fig.width)
  theme_update(plot.caption = element_markdown(size = size))
  bayesplot_theme_update(plot.caption = element_markdown(size = size))
  options
})

# `note`, if given, sits on the left of the social caption's row
post_table <- function(table, note = NULL) {
  footer <- if (is.null(note)) {
    socials
  } else {
    str_glue(
      "<div style='display:flex; flex-wrap:wrap; justify-content:space-between; ",
      "align-items:baseline; gap:4px 16px;'>",
      "<span style='flex:1 1 200px; color:#666666; text-align:left;'>{note}</span>",
      "<span style='margin-left:auto;'>{socials}</span></div>"
    )
  }

  table |>
    opt_table_font(font = list(google_font("Poppins"), default_fonts())) |>
    opt_align_table_header(align = "left") |>
    tab_options(
      table.width = pct(100),
      table.font.size = px(14),
      table.font.color = "#1F2937",
      table.background.color = "white",
      table.border.top.style = "none",
      table.border.bottom.style = "none",
      heading.title.font.size = px(18),
      heading.subtitle.font.size = px(13),
      heading.border.bottom.style = "none",
      heading.padding = px(2),
      column_labels.font.size = px(11),
      column_labels.font.weight = "600",
      column_labels.text_transform = "uppercase",
      column_labels.border.top.style = "none",
      column_labels.border.bottom.width = px(2),
      column_labels.border.bottom.color = navy,
      table_body.hlines.color = "#E8ECF1",
      table_body.border.top.style = "none",
      table_body.border.bottom.style = "none",
      row_group.as_column = TRUE,
      row_group.border.top.width = px(1),
      row_group.border.top.color = "#9FB3CE",
      row_group.border.bottom.style = "none",
      stub_row_group.border.style = "none",
      row_group.font.size = px(12),
      data_row.padding = px(9),
      quarto.disable_processing = TRUE
    ) |>
    tab_style(
      style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
      locations = cells_title("title")
    ) |>
    tab_style(
      style = cell_text(color = "grey40"),
      locations = list(cells_title("subtitle"), cells_column_labels())
    ) |>
    tab_style(
      style = "letter-spacing: 0.05em;",
      locations = cells_column_labels()
    ) |>
    # The group a set of rows belongs to, as a block of the charts' pale navy
    tab_style(
      style = list(
        cell_fill("#EEF3F9"),
        cell_text(color = navy, weight = "600")
      ),
      locations = cells_row_groups()
    ) |>
    # Digits of equal width, so columns of numbers line up
    tab_style(
      style = list(
        cell_text(v_align = "middle"),
        "font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums;"
      ),
      locations = cells_body()
    ) |>
    # Each group's name sits in the middle of its block, and a rule runs across
    # the whole row where a new group starts
    tab_style(
      style = cell_text(v_align = "middle"),
      locations = cells_row_groups()
    ) |>
    opt_css(
      "
      .gt_table tr.gt_row_group_first td {
        border-top: 1px solid #9FB3CE !important;
      }
    "
    ) |>
    tab_source_note(source_note = html(footer)) |>
    # Set the social caption apart from the last row above it
    tab_style(
      style = list(cell_text(align = "right"), "padding-top: 16px;"),
      locations = cells_source_notes()
    ) |>
    tab_options(source_notes.font.size = px(13))
}

pill <- function(text, colour, background) {
  str_glue(
    "<span style='display:inline-block; padding:2px 10px; border-radius:999px; ",
    "font-weight:600; white-space:nowrap; color:{colour}; ",
    "background:{background};'>{text}</span>"
  ) |>
    as.character()
}

# The colours the videos use for a probability, darkened to read on white
probability_pill <- function(probability, text) {
  pill(
    text,
    colour = case_when(
      probability < 0.5 ~ "#B4122B",
      probability < 0.7 ~ "#92400E",
      .default = "#166534"
    ),
    background = case_when(
      probability < 0.5 ~ "#FCE4E8",
      probability < 0.7 ~ "#FEF3C7",
      .default = "#DCFCE7"
    )
  )
}

# Where one play sits among all of them, by rank: a dot on a track running from
# the lowest-ranked play (left) to the highest (right), with a tick at the
# middle play
range_dot <- function(percentile) {
  str_glue(
    "<div style='position:relative; height:16px; min-width:110px;'>",
    "<div style='position:absolute; top:7px; left:0; right:0; height:2px; ",
    "background:#D5DCE6; border-radius:1px;'></div>",
    "<div style='position:absolute; top:3px; left:50%; width:1px; ",
    "height:10px; background:#94A3B8;'></div>",
    "<div style='position:absolute; top:1px; ",
    "left:calc({round(percentile)}% - 7px); width:14px; height:14px; ",
    "box-sizing:border-box; border-radius:50%; background:{navy}; ",
    "border:2px solid white;'></div>",
    "</div>"
  )
}
